name: Irving Katz
bio: Irving Katz was one of the nine Philadelphia Communist leaders convicted in 1953 under the Smith Act. On November 13, 1957 the Third Circuit Court of Appeals, applying the Supreme Court's Yates decision, set aside his conviction along with several co-defendants'.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1953; conviction set aside on appeal November 1957
sentence: Convicted under the Smith Act; reversed after Yates

name: Robert Klonsky
bio: Robert Klonsky was one of the nine Philadelphia Smith Act defendants convicted in 1953. The Third Circuit ordered a new trial for him in November 1957 under the Yates standard; the defendants called a retrial 'a travesty of justice.'
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Joseph Roberts
bio: Joseph Roberts was one of the nine Philadelphia Communist leaders convicted under the Smith Act in 1953 and granted a new trial by the Third Circuit Court of Appeals in November 1957 following the Yates decision.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: William Borders
bio: The Rev. William Holmes Borders was a prominent Atlanta minister and president of the Love, Law and Liberation Movement, one of six Black ministers arrested in January 1957 for deliberately riding in the 'white' seats of an Atlanta bus to create a court test of segregation. He was fingerprinted and released on bond and faced grand-jury indictment.

name: Charles Gomillion
bio: Charles G. Gomillion was a Tuskegee Institute dean and president of the Tuskegee Civic Association, who in 1957 led a Black boycott of white merchants protesting a state gerrymander that stripped almost all Black voters from the city. He was enjoined under Alabama's anti-boycott law, his offices were raided in a 'subversive activities' probe, and arrests were threatened; he went on to win the landmark voting case Gomillion v. Lightfoot (1960).
charges: Alabama anti-boycott law (injunction) — for leading the Tuskegee boycott

name: Grady Jenkins
bio: Grady Jenkins was a New Orleans maritime worker and civil-rights activist arrested in early 1957 under Louisiana's criminal-anarchy and anti-subversion laws after he and his wife refused to answer the Eastland Senate subcommittee. Suffering from tuberculosis, he was shackled to his hospital bed when arrested; his defense argued the state laws were void under the Supreme Court's Nelson ruling.
sentence: Held on bail; faced up to 20 years

name: Judy Jenkins
bio: Judy Jenkins was a New Orleans civil-rights activist arrested with her husband Grady in 1957 under Louisiana's criminal-anarchy and anti-subversion laws for refusing to answer the Eastland subcommittee. The couple, parents of two small children, were prosecuted in what supporters called a Red-scare diversion tied to segregation politics.
sentence: Held on bail; faced up to 20 years

name: Daisy Bates
bio: Daisy Bates was the president of the Arkansas NAACP and the mentor of the Little Rock Nine, arrested in November 1957 for the NAACP's refusal to hand over its membership lists under a new Little Rock city ordinance — part of Arkansas's drive to cripple the organization amid the Central High desegregation fight. She surrendered to police and was released on bond.
charges: Violating a Little Rock ordinance requiring disclosure of NAACP membership lists
sentence: Released on $300 bond; appealed (later won in the Supreme Court)

name: J. C. Crenshaw
bio: The Rev. J. C. Crenshaw was the president of the Little Rock NAACP branch, arrested with Daisy Bates in November 1957 for the organization's refusal to disclose its membership and finances under a city ordinance — part of the campaign against the NAACP during the Little Rock school-integration crisis.
charges: Violating a Little Rock ordinance requiring disclosure of NAACP membership lists

name: Augustus J. Johnson
bio: Augustus J. Johnson was a New York City subway motorman, a leader of the Motormen's Benevolent Association and of the United African Nationalist Movement, jailed in late 1957 for his part in leading the New York subway (motormen's) strike.
charges: Jailed for leading the New York subway motormen's strike

name: Lawrence Ferlinghetti
bio: Lawrence Ferlinghetti was the poet and proprietor of San Francisco's City Lights Bookshop, prosecuted in 1957 under California obscenity law for publishing and selling Allen Ginsberg's 'Howl and Other Poems.' The landmark trial ended in acquittal that fall, a major victory for literary free expression.
charges: Obscenity — for publishing and selling 'Howl and Other Poems'

name: Shigeyoshi Murao
bio: Shigeyoshi Murao was a clerk at the City Lights Bookshop, arrested and tried with Lawrence Ferlinghetti in 1957 under California obscenity law for selling Ginsberg's 'Howl.' The prosecution offered no evidence he knew the book's content, and the case ended in acquittal.
charges: Obscenity — for selling 'Howl and Other Poems'
